prompt: A purchase fails somewhere between the button and the confirmation. Which question does the whole-system view tell you to ask first?

options.text: Which boundary did not preserve the intended request, identity, data, or response
Which process raised the error, since that is where the failure happened
options.feedback: A process is where a failure surfaced, which is not the same as where the intended thing stopped being preserved. A web app is the coordinated behaviour of the arrangement, not any single process.

options.text: Whether the fault is on the browser side or the server side
options.feedback: A typical interaction crosses presentation code, network infrastructure, server-side application logic and one or more data systems. Two sides are not enough categories to hold the answer.

options.text: Which component is at fault, so that component can be fixed
options.feedback: Naming a component only searches the boxes. Every arrow between them is a contract and a possible failure boundary too, and a question about boxes never reaches those.

explanation: What the map buys is a first question with an owner attached: which boundary did not preserve the intended request, identity, data, or response. Naming a process, a side or a component answers something narrower than what was asked.

prompt: Match each responsibility to the part of the arrangement that holds it.

pairs.left: Presents documents and controls, and sends protocol messages
Terminates secure connections and routes traffic
Validates requests and coordinates business behaviour

explanation: Each part answers for one kind of thing, which is what makes “which boundary did not preserve what” a question anybody can act on. The two distractors are genuine participants — a backend publishes follow-up work to a queue and is a client to a payment API — but neither of them owns any of the five responsibilities listed here.

prompt: Order the steps of one purchase, from the browser's first move to the updated screen.

steps.text: Browser sends an HTTP request with session credentials
Backend authenticates the caller, then authorizes the action
Backend validates input, then executes a transaction
Backend publishes follow-up work and returns a representation
Frontend reconciles the response with local state and updates the page

explanation: Two things in that order are easy to lose. Identity is established before the action is authorized and before the input is validated, so both of those run on a caller who has already been identified. And the exchange is not finished when the representation is returned: published follow-up work lands in a system the response need not mention, and the frontend still has to reconcile what came back.

prompt: A dependency is overloaded and calls to it are timing out. Someone proposes retrying every failed call automatically. What does that proposal risk?

options.text: Amplifying the overload, and duplicating effects
Nothing — the calls failed, so there is nothing to duplicate
options.feedback: A call that failed for the caller is not a call that did nothing. Duplicate submissions and partial writes are both on the list of common failures.

options.text: Expired certificates, because each retry renegotiates the connection
options.feedback: Expired certificates are a common failure, but nothing here connects them to retrying. Taking any entry off the list is not the same as reasoning about this one.

options.text: Changing one side of a contract before the other
options.feedback: That is a deployment failure mode. A retry repeats a message; it does not change a contract.

explanation: A retry can repair transient failure, or amplify overload and duplicate effects — one mechanism with both outcomes available. With the dependency already overloaded, amplification is the outcome the proposal invites.

prompt: A team moves confirmation work out of the request and into a background job — one more boundary. What does that boundary charge for the independent change it enables?

options.text: Latency
Failure modes
Security policy
Operational work
Independent change or scale
Fewer parts to operate

explanation: An added boundary enables independent change or scale, and it adds latency, failure modes, security policy, and operational work. The two wrong options are the other side of that trade: independent change or scale is what the boundary buys rather than what it costs, and it is bought with operational work rather than by reducing it.

back: A distributed system with a human-facing browser interface. A typical interaction crosses presentation code, network infrastructure, server-side application logic, and one or more data systems, and the visible page is only the edge of it.

Each arrow between the parts is a contract and a possible failure boundary — the half of the map the boxes hide. A component may play several roles across those arrows: a backend is a server to the browser and a client to a database or a payment API.
HTTP defines the uniform semantics shared across its versions, which is why one trace can describe the exchange without naming a version.

Server-rendered or client-rendered UI, a synchronous request or a background job, a relational database or another model, one deployable unit or several services, a managed platform or self-operated infrastructure — the important choices are choices about where the boundaries go.

front: A success response is not the outcome
back: For `POST /orders`, correctness may require a durable order, exactly one charge effect, inventory policy, a traceable audit record, and a UI state that distinguishes “pending” from “failed”. The web app is the coordinated behaviour, not any single process.

prompt: A host answers packets and accepts a connection, but the page still will not load. What have those two checks established?

options.text: That the network path is clean end to end
options.feedback: Two successful samples are not a clean path — packet loss and connection exhaustion are still on the list of things that go wrong. And even a flawless path would say nothing about HTTP.

options.text: Routing and basic reachability, but nothing about HTTP behaviour
That DNS is configured correctly, since the host responded
options.feedback: You reached it by address, so name resolution was never exercised. DNS is still a suspect.

options.text: That the application is up and the browser is at fault
options.feedback: A web app can be unavailable even when its host is perfectly reachable. Nothing here has looked at the app yet.

explanation: Each check proves a property of one layer and the layers below it. A network can deliver packets while an HTTP request fails, so reachability says nothing about whether HTTP behaviour is correct.

prompt: HTTP is defined as a stateless application-level request-response protocol. What does that make the login session your app keeps?

options.text: An added mechanism, built on top of a protocol that carries nothing between requests
A feature of HTTP that switches on once the user authenticates
options.feedback: Statelessness is not a mode HTTP leaves. Whatever continuity your app has between requests, your app added it.

options.text: A property of the transport connection underneath
options.feedback: A transport connection associates endpoint addresses and ports. Application state is not its job, and connections may be short-lived by design.

options.text: A sign that the app has been built incorrectly
options.feedback: Sessions are normal and necessary. The point is only that they sit above HTTP rather than inside it.

explanation: HTTP is explicitly stateless, so application sessions are something built on top of it. That is also why “how much application state is coupled to a particular process” is a live design decision rather than a settled one.

prompt: Match each decision a developer makes to the layer of the stack it is made at.

pairs.left: How much state is coupled to one process

explanation: Naming the layer a decision belongs to is most of what the stack is for. None of these four decisions lands on routing or the physical network, which is why those two appear here only as distractors.

back: The internet is a network of interconnected networks, moving packets between interfaces. The web is an application system built on that connectivity, using URLs to identify resources, HTTP to exchange representations, and browsers as general-purpose clients.
HTTP is explicitly a stateless application-level request-response protocol, so nothing in it carries information from one request to the next. Application sessions are an added mechanism on top.
The distributed hierarchy that resolves names to addresses. It is the step a request that works by IP but not by name never got to exercise.

front: A reasoning stack, not an implementation
back: The layer diagram is a reasoning tool, not a claim that every implementation has identical layers. What it fixes is the direction of dependence: each layer relies on services below it and exposes a narrower abstraction above. The same dependence runs through a page load, which is why one step can fail on its own terms while the rest look healthy.
More intermediaries can improve reach, security and caching, and the same intermediaries complicate diagnosis and trust — proxy policy being one of the ways a request fails.

prompt: Order the six messages of one request-response exchange.

steps.text: Frontend to edge: request, credentials and trace context
Backend to data store: query or transaction
Backend to edge: status, headers and content

explanation: The request travels down the participants and the response comes back up the same three hops. Every one of the six is a place the exchange can stop — the three on the way back no less than the three on the way out.

prompt: Match each responsibility to the participant that holds it.

pairs.left: Attach headers and apply credential rules
Terminate TLS or serve a cached representation
Answer a query or run a transaction

explanation: Naming the participant that owns a responsibility is what makes a boundary check possible: an edge that serves a cached representation means the backend never saw the message at all. DNS resolution and connection pooling are in the path too, but they are work that may not happen — reused from caches or pools — rather than participants that decide anything about the message.

prompt: A checkout has a two-second user deadline. Which of these follow from budgeting the path end to end rather than hop by hop?

options.text: Reserve a portion of the two seconds for connection, edge, application, database and response transfer
Refuse to start a five-second payment call once 1.8 seconds have already gone
Give every hop its own two-second timeout so no single hop is the bottleneck
Retry any request that overruns its portion, so the user still gets an answer

explanation: Deadlines are chosen end to end, not independently at every hop. Per-hop timeouts that are each generous on their own terms are how a path ends up with no budget at all, which rules out the third option. The fourth ignores two constraints at once: a blanket retry is how retry storms start, and retrying an operation that is neither idempotent nor queryable can commit the work twice.

prompt: Requests are slow, but the application's own timing shows it handling them quickly. Which part of the path does that point at?
hints: The application only starts its clock once it has the request.
The time went somewhere before the code you instrumented.
explanation: Queueing before application code is a standard failure mode, and it hides from application timing by definition — the clock the application keeps starts after the wait is already over. The symptom eliminates application logic and points at whatever held the request before it.

back: A request carries a method and a target; a response carries a status and optional content. Credentials, trace context, caching and deadlines are arrangement built around those two messages rather than parts of them.

A retry that reuses the same idempotency key lets the server return the original outcome instead of doing the work a second time. It is what turns a timeout from an unknown outcome into a question you can ask again.
Streaming reduces time to first content and complicates error replacement: once content has started arriving, an error can no longer simply replace it.
Caching saves work and adds invalidation and privacy rules. Both obligations arrive with the saving, not later.
A `200` response can still contain the wrong business result. The status describes the exchange, not the correctness of the outcome carried inside it.

prompt: An HTTP origin is distinguished by scheme, host and port. Which of these changes leaves the origin the same?

options.text: Changing the path from `/orders` to `/orders/open`
Changing the scheme from `http` to `https`
options.feedback: The scheme is part of the origin, so those are two different origins even though the host and the path never moved.

options.text: Moving the app from `app.example.com` to `www.example.com`
options.feedback: The host is part of the origin. This is the migration that touches DNS records, certificates, cookie scope and everything else defined on an origin.

options.text: Serving the same host on a different port
options.feedback: The port is part of the origin too. All three of scheme, host and port have to match.

explanation: Scheme, host and port make an origin; the path and the query do not. That is why moving a resource within a host is cheap and moving it to another host is not.

prompt: Query parameters are appropriate for selecting a representation and unsafe for secrets. What property of URLs makes them unsafe?
accept: they appear in logs and history
URLs appear in logs and history
they end up in logs and history
hints: Think about where a URL is written down after the request is over.
Two places keep it: one on the server side, one in the browser.
explanation: URLs appear in logs and history, so anything in the query outlives the request in places nobody audited. The path and query being addressed to the application does not make them private.

prompt: A DNS record was changed an hour ago, and some clients still reach the old address. What does that show?

options.text: Resolution can follow caches and delegated name servers, so nothing guarantees a change is instantly global
The change was applied incorrectly, since DNS is authoritative
options.feedback: An authoritative record is not the same thing as the answer a client currently holds. Caches and delegated name servers sit between the two.

options.text: The old server is refusing to give up the name
options.feedback: Servers do not hold names. What is holding the old answer is the resolution path, not the machine at the end of it.

options.text: A shorter time-to-live would have made the change instant
options.feedback: Short TTLs speed routing changes and increase lookup traffic — and still never guarantee instant global change.

explanation: DNS resolution can follow caches and delegated name servers, so an answer describes what some resolver holds rather than what is authoritative right now. Short TTLs shift the tradeoff — faster routing changes, more lookup traffic — without ever guaranteeing instant global change.

prompt: Match each symptom to the mechanism it implicates.

pairs.left: The name still resolves to the old address
The certificate is not valid for this host
A forwarded host field is trusted unchecked
One page loads content over both schemes

explanation: Each symptom narrows to one of the four cooperating mechanisms rather than to all of them. Mixed HTTP and HTTPS content is the one people misfile: it implicates the scheme in the URLs a page emits, not the server that served the page. Cookie scope and OAuth redirect URIs are things an origin migration breaks, but no symptom listed here points at either.

back: Negotiates cryptographic parameters, and is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery.
Many requests may share one connection without sharing application meaning. A connection is a pipe, not a session.
They improve linking and caching, which is why a path worth publishing is a path worth keeping.
Moving a host touches DNS records, certificates, cookie scope, CORS policy, OAuth redirect URIs, canonical links, caches and monitoring — an origin migration, not a text replacement.

Convenient, and it moves the boundary: the internal hops past the edge still need an explicit trust model of their own. And the certificate itself proves control of a name under the certificate system, not that the application behind it is benign.

prompt: `GET /reports/monthly` returned a cached PDF last week and a redirect to object storage today. What changed?

options.text: The representation and its delivery, while the resource stayed the same
The resource, since a redirect is a different kind of thing from a document
options.feedback: The resource is the conceptual target the URI identifies. It is still the monthly report — a redirect is one more way of delivering a representation of it.

options.text: Nothing a client can observe, so the difference does not matter
options.feedback: A client certainly observes it. The point is not that the change is invisible; it is that the change was the server's to make.

options.text: The identifier's meaning, which now names object storage
options.feedback: The URL still names the monthly report. Had it named the storage, this migration would have changed the identifier too — which is the failure the design exists to avoid.

explanation: A resource is the conceptual target identified by a URI; a representation is transferable information about that resource. The current representation and its delivery mechanism are separate design decisions, so changing them is not changing the resource.

prompt: Match each design choice to what it buys and what it costs.
distractors: Stable nouns and generic HTTP behavior
explanation: Each choice buys something at a stated price, and none of them has a default answer. Server authority is the one whose price you have to read off its alternative: what it gives up is the responsiveness optimistic client state can buy. The two distractors are real benefits — of resource-oriented and action-oriented designs respectively — but they belong to the choice of style, not to any of the four tradeoffs listed here.

prompt: Which of these break a client even though the server's own code is correct?

options.text: A URL that encoded an implementation detail which later changed
A status code that does not match the outcome
A representation that silently omits information needed to interpret it
An account assembled from several stores rather than read from one row
A response format changing from HTML to JSON under content negotiation

explanation: The first three are failures of the boundary rather than of the logic behind it: the client was told something untrue, or told too little, or made to depend on a detail it should never have seen. The last two are the arrangement working — HTTP deliberately hides resource implementation, and negotiating a format is what content negotiation is for. A client that breaks on either had inferred undocumented behaviour.

back: The method communicates the requested action; the target names what the action concerns.

Clients select methods, targets, fields and acceptable formats. Servers interpret those semantics, enforce policy, and choose a status and a representation. Both are roles in one interaction rather than kinds of machine: the same process is a server to a browser and a client to a payment provider.
Content negotiation, conditional requests, redirects and caching let a single resource model support different clients and efficient reuse.
It can represent an account assembled from several stores, calculated at request time, and formatted as HTML or JSON, all without the identifier changing.

Resource implementation, behind messages and representations — the uniform boundary that lets independently implemented components interoperate. It can hide multiplicity too: what you call the server may be a chain of proxies and services with different policy.

prompt: Match each stage of the rendering pipeline to what it produces.
explanation: Each stage has one product, and naming it is what lets you place a symptom at a stage rather than at “the browser”. The two distractors are real, but neither belongs to a stage: default semantics and keyboard behaviour are what native elements contribute, and pixels together with accessibility information are what the whole pipeline turns network-delivered resources and application state into.

prompt: A gallery ships with images that declare no width or height, off-screen slides moved out of view by a style rather than removed from the tree, and a script that looks up its nodes before the markup below has been parsed. It never measures layout. Which problems does that page invite?

options.text: Cumulative layout shift, because dimensions stay unknown until the late-loading images arrive
Null references or flashes, from an invalid assumption about element timing
Content that is visually hidden yet still exposed to assistive technology
Layout thrashing, from alternating DOM writes and measurements
Paint produced before layout, so the drawing operations never composite

explanation: The first three are named failure modes and this page walks into each one: dimensions unknown until late-loading resources arrive, an assumption about when an element exists, and content that is visually hidden while still exposed to assistive technology. Layout thrashing alternates DOM writes and measurements, and this page never measures layout, so that failure is not available to it. And paint cannot come before layout: the pipeline derives sizes and positions before it produces drawing operations.

prompt: A gallery component adds a class to each thumbnail and then reads that thumbnail's height, one after another down the list. Which change removes the forced synchronization?

options.text: Write every class first, then measure once the batch is done
Read each height before writing its class, rather than after
options.feedback: The alternation is the problem, not its direction. Writes and measurements are still interleaved, and every read still follows the previous write.

options.text: Reserve a width and height for every thumbnail
options.feedback: Reserved dimensions stop late-loading resources from shifting content. They do not change how often this loop makes the browser synchronize work.

options.text: Render fewer thumbnails, so the tree the loop walks is smaller
options.feedback: A smaller tree lowers traversal, style, memory and accessibility costs, and the loop still alternates a write with a measurement at every step.

explanation: Layout thrashing alternates DOM writes and measurements, and reading layout immediately after writing styles may force the browser to synchronize work. The rebuilt gallery batches DOM updates and measures layout after the batch — the only one of these four changes that stops the alternating.

back: An API-facing tree, not the screen. Rendering turns network-delivered resources and application state into pixels and accessibility information, and those two outputs can disagree: content can be visually hidden yet exposed to assistive technology, or the reverse.
They contribute default semantics and keyboard behaviour. Native controls are less customizable but bring robust behaviour, so replacing one with a custom control trades those defaults for design.

front: What the HTML standard leaves open
back: It specifies document behaviour and offers default rendering guidance while allowing user agents implementation freedom, which is why browsers may stream and overlap the rendering stages rather than running them in strict turns.
Server-rendered HTML can expose meaningful content early; client rendering can support rich local interaction but requires code and data before completion.
It simplifies “render everything” logic while increasing traversal, style, memory, and accessibility costs.

prompt: Put one turn of the event loop in order.
explanation: The chain is the loop's own: take a task, run JavaScript to completion, drain eligible microtasks, allow rendering and host work, take another task. The order is why long tasks delay input and rendering — the fourth step waits on the second — and why a loop that continually enqueues microtasks can starve other work at the third.

prompt: A page stops repainting and stops responding to input, yet nothing it runs takes more than a fraction of a millisecond. What is happening?
accept: a loop that continually enqueues microtasks
a loop that keeps enqueuing microtasks
hints: Rendering and host work get their turn at only one point in the loop.
Something is refilling a queue that has to be emptied before that point is reached.
explanation: A loop that continually enqueues microtasks can starve other work. Eligible jobs are drained before the loop allows rendering and host work, so a queue that refills itself never lets the turn reach that step — and because every individual job is short, nothing here looks like a long task. The symptom rules the obvious cause out rather than confirming it.

prompt: A loader awaits the profile, then awaits the settings, then awaits the notifications. None of the three depends on the others. What has that bought, and what has it spent?

options.text: Sequential readability, at the cost of accidentally serializing three independent operations
Explicit dependency order, at the cost of cancelling the other two if one fails
options.feedback: Promises do make dependency order explicit, but they do not cancel underlying work by themselves, and nothing here cancels anything.

options.text: Neither — `await` is how a promise is consumed, and the three still proceed together
options.feedback: `async`/`await` improves sequential readability while accidentally serializing independent operations if used carelessly. Awaiting each in turn is that carelessness.

options.text: Responsiveness, at the cost of moving the work off this agent
options.feedback: Moving work off the agent is what workers do, and they add serialization, lifecycle and coordination overhead of their own. Nothing here leaves the agent.

explanation: `async`/`await` improves sequential readability while accidentally serializing independent operations if used carelessly. These three have no dependency between them, so the sequence is paid for in elapsed time and buys only the shape of the source.

back: The language defines values, functions, execution contexts, modules, promises, and jobs. The browser supplies DOM, timers, networking, events, and an event loop that schedules host work.
ECMAScript jobs run only when no other execution context is active, and a started job runs to completion. It protects one job from interruption and says nothing about which job runs first.
examples: Ecma International, ECMAScript Language Specification: Jobs

back: Closures retain lexical bindings. A stale closure is that same mechanism read later: a callback running against the values it captured rather than the current ones.
Promises make dependency order explicit but do not cancel underlying work by themselves, which is why a search box has to discard an older answer on arrival rather than prevent it.
Separate agents with message-based coordination and constrained shared memory. They preserve UI responsiveness for CPU-heavy tasks but add serialization, lifecycle, and coordination overhead.

prompt: Match each fact the news app holds to the store it is kept in.
explanation: Each placement answers the same five axes — lifetime, sensitivity, size, consistency and server visibility. Article assets are reusable responses; the theme is simple client state kept locally because losing it is acceptable; saved-reading metadata is larger structured client data; account state has to agree with the server, so the server is authority for it. Both distractors are real mechanisms that this app does not use for these four facts: a secure, HTTP-only cookie is where a server session identifier belongs when frontend code does not need to read it, and a service-worker cache is a programmable resource cache the worker itself decides about.

prompt: An app writes an offline save to IndexedDB and immediately shows it to the reader as saved. Which assumption has it made that the platform does not support?

options.text: That local data is durable — browsers may evict storage under pressure, and users can clear it
That IndexedDB can hold larger structured client data
options.feedback: It can; that is its primary use. What fails here is a claim about permanence rather than about shape.

options.text: That the browser will keep the stored record in the same shape across releases
options.feedback: Versioning stored schemas is the application's job, and nothing in this scenario changes the schema. The claim that fails is “saved”.

options.text: That origin-scoped storage keeps other sites out
options.feedback: Origin-scoped APIs do prevent arbitrary sites from reading one another's state. That is a promise the platform makes rather than one it withholds.

explanation: Assuming local data is durable is one of the named mistakes: browsers may evict storage under pressure, and users can clear it. The news app is careful about exactly this — offline saves carry unique operation IDs and display “pending sync” until acknowledged, which is a weaker and truer claim than “saved”.

prompt: A team adds an offline mutation queue so readers can act without a connection. Which obligations does that take on?

options.text: Conflict rules, for work the server has already seen differently
Retry rules, for work that has to be attempted again later
Identity rules, so an operation can be recognised when it is sent again
A guarantee that the queue survives until the connection returns
Presenting queued work as already applied, so the interface stays simple

explanation: Offline mutation queues improve resilience but require conflict, retry, and identity rules — three obligations that arrive with the feature rather than later. The fourth option is not on offer: browsers may evict storage under pressure and users can clear it, so nothing guarantees the queue survives. The fifth is a named mistake, presenting stale offline data as current; the news app displays “pending sync” until the server acknowledges instead.

back: Between volatile frontend memory and authoritative server data. It is generally partitioned and governed by origin and browser policy, and it is not an unlimited local database.

front: Which stores travel with a request
back: The HTTP cache is applied by fetch machinery and cookies go according to cookie policy. Session and local storage and IndexedDB are not sent automatically, and for a service-worker cache the worker decides.
HTTP freshness can avoid revalidation; validators allow conditional requests.

Origin-scoped APIs prevent arbitrary sites from reading one another's state. They do not coordinate an origin with itself: multiple tabs can update shared origin storage without application-level coordination.
It improves latency while raising staleness and invalidation costs.

prompt: The network panel records a response arriving; the script that made the call has an error and no data. Which step of the browser's algorithm accounts for the gap?

options.text: Filtering the response for the caller
Applying credentials, origin and cache policy
options.feedback: Policy is applied while the request is being constructed and sent, and this request was sent — the panel recorded a response coming back. What the caller receives is decided after that.

options.text: Resolving or reusing the connection
options.feedback: A connection was resolved and the response travelled over it. Connection pools amortize DNS, transport and TLS work; none of that withholds a body.

options.text: Following the network and redirects
options.feedback: That step ended with a response arriving, which is exactly what the panel records. The gap opens after it.

explanation: Application code requests a resource; the browser applies a larger security and protocol algorithm whose last step filters the response for the caller. That is why a request seen in developer tools may differ from application options, and why a server response can arrive on the network yet remain unavailable to frontend code.

prompt: A reader navigates away and the dashboard aborts its in-flight fetches. Which of these are true of that abort?

options.text: It communicates that the caller no longer needs the result
The server may already be processing the request
A mutation already under way is governed by idempotency and server-side deadlines rather than by the abort
The server has stopped working on the request
The response body may now be consumed a second time

explanation: Abort signals communicate that a caller no longer needs a result, though the server may already be processing it — and the dashboard is explicit about the division: navigating away aborts local interest, while idempotency and server-side deadlines govern any mutation already in progress. Treating abort as proof the server stopped is a named failure, and consuming a response body twice is a separate one that an abort does nothing to license.

prompt: A dashboard that fetched three data sets concurrently is changed to fetch twelve from the same origin, and elapsed time gets worse. What happened?

options.text: Parallel fetches reduce elapsed time until connection, server, or client limits turn them into contention
The fetches serialized, because a browser runs one fetch at a time
options.feedback: Navigation, subresource loading and script-initiated fetches share infrastructure, and connection pools exist so concurrent work can reuse connections. Concurrency is not what was removed.

options.text: CORS checks ran twelve times instead of three
options.feedback: CORS is a browser rule about exposing selected cross-origin responses to scripts, and these fetches are same-origin. Nothing here crosses an origin.

options.text: The waterfall grew, because each fetch had to discover the next
options.feedback: Waterfalls are caused by discovering critical resources late, and these twelve were all started together. That is contention rather than a waterfall.

explanation: Parallel fetches reduce elapsed time until connection, server, or client limits turn them into contention. The ceiling has three possible owners — the connections, the server, or the client — which is why the dashboard keeps to three independent data sets and gives each one a deadline and a visible partial-error state.

back: CORS is a browser rule that lets a server opt into exposing selected cross-origin responses to scripts. It is not server authentication.
They amortize DNS, transport, and TLS work, which is why resolving a connection is often reusing one that already exists.

front: Three kinds of fetch, one infrastructure
back: Navigation, subresource loading, and script-initiated fetches share infrastructure but have different destinations and policy.

front: Why a browser error says so little
back: Browser errors often intentionally omit security-sensitive details from scripts, so a thin message is policy rather than a defect.
Prefetching hides latency but spends bandwidth and may trigger unwanted work.

prompt: The order table needs to show how many orders match the current filter. The orders arrive as input and the filter lives in query state. Where should that count live?

options.text: Nowhere — derive it from the orders and the query whenever it is wanted
In local state, refreshed by an effect whenever the orders or the query change
options.feedback: That stores a fact two other facts already imply. Duplicated derived state drifts from its source, and the refresh becomes one more thing that can fail to run — which is the caption above the nine rows.

options.text: In a central store, so any screen that needs the count can read it
options.feedback: Central stores simplify cross-cutting coordination, and this count coordinates nothing outside the table. Global state can outlive the user or route it belonged to, which is a poor trade for a number you can compute.

options.text: As an input, computed by the layer that supplies the orders
options.feedback: Inputs pass data into a component, so this would be recomputed upstream every time the filter changed — for a value already computable from what the table holds.

explanation: Derived state is computed from authoritative inputs, which is what makes “what can be derived instead of stored” the third question the model hands you. Storing the answer instead creates a second copy of a fact, and duplicated derived state drifts from its source.

prompt: A reader is halfway through typing a note into a row of a long table when a background refresh reorders the rows. Their text is gone. What is the cause?
hints: Nothing about the note changed. What changed is which component the system thinks it is looking at.
The same failure loses focus as well as input.
explanation: Unstable identity loses input or focus. A component the system treats as a new one arrives holding none of the transient interaction state the old one held — and local state is exactly what supports transient interaction. The note was never in the authoritative order data, so nothing upstream could put it back.

prompt: Match each part of the order table to its role in the data flow.

pairs.right: an input passed in from above

pairs.left: Which row the reader has expanded
The rows left after the filter

distractors: shared state coordinating siblings or routes
scattered DOM mutation the table performs itself
explanation: Inputs pass data into a component; events or callbacks communicate outward. Local state supports transient interaction and derived state is computed from authoritative inputs, which between them account for everything the table holds. Nothing here is shared state, because the table coordinates no sibling and no route, and none of it is scattered DOM mutation — the thing predictable data flow replaces.

back: Components group presentation and interaction around a responsibility. State records information that can change. Reactivity keeps rendered output and derived behavior synchronized with those state changes.
The browser remains the actual rendering platform; a component system schedules and applies DOM changes rather than becoming the thing that draws.
Colocating state with its smallest owner improves comprehension. Central stores simplify cross-cutting coordination but can turn unrelated changes into global coupling.
Reactive systems detect dependencies through explicit subscriptions, compiler analysis, signals, or rerender-and-diff strategies.
Immutable updates simplify change detection and history; fine-grained mutable signals can reduce work but require disciplined ownership.

prompt: A project board has a status filter that readers paste into chat messages, and a half-written comment that must not turn up in anyone's history. Where does each belong?

options.text: The filter in the query; the comment somewhere other than the URL
Both in the query, so that a refresh restores the reader's exact position
options.feedback: The URL is the serialized, public portion of navigation state. Whatever goes there is durable and shareable whether or not you wanted it to be, and a half-written comment is neither.

options.text: The filter in the path; the comment in the fragment
options.feedback: The path selects a resource or screen and the fragment identifies a position within the resulting document. A filter selects a view, which is the query's job — and the fragment is still part of the URL.

options.text: Both outside the URL, with the filter restored from the router's own state
options.feedback: That hides navigation inside transient component state, which is what routing exists to avoid. A filter kept there is not linkable, refreshable or shareable.

explanation: Put durable, shareable filters in the query and sensitive or ephemeral data elsewhere. Good routing makes application state linkable, refreshable, shareable, and compatible with browser history rather than hiding navigation inside transient component state — and the same publicity that buys all four is why the comment cannot go there.

prompt: Put the client navigation from `/orders` to `/orders/123` in order.

steps.text: Move focus to the detail heading

explanation: Navigating from `/orders` to `/orders/123` pushes a history entry, renders a pending region, loads order `123`, then moves focus to the detail heading. The order is the argument: the history entry comes first because the browser owns session history and the back button has to work from the moment the address changes, and focus moves last because until the detail heading exists there is nowhere to move it to.

prompt: A documentation site has to serve readers whose devices never run the application's JavaScript. Which routing choice does that force, and what is given up?

options.text: Server routing — it works without application JavaScript and gives each response an independent lifecycle, at the cost of the shell state and fluid transitions client routing preserves
Client routing — it preserves shell state and enables fluid transitions, and the router can fall back to the server when JavaScript is unavailable
options.feedback: A frontend router is application JavaScript. If none runs, there is no router to fall back from.

options.text: Either — the two differ in how a navigation feels rather than in what it requires
options.feedback: Server routing works without application JavaScript. Client navigation updates history and fetches or reveals the next screen through client-side code, which is a requirement rather than a preference.

options.text: Server routing — and nothing is given up, since client routing has to reproduce document-level concerns anyway
options.feedback: Reproducing document-level concerns is a cost on client routing's side of the ledger, not a cancellation of what it buys. Preserved shell state and fluid transitions are what you are giving up.

explanation: Server routing works without application JavaScript and gives each response an independent lifecycle. Client routing preserves shell state and enables fluid transitions but must reproduce document-level concerns — restoring titles, focus, and scroll among them. The constraint settles which one you take; the ledger is what you should be able to state afterwards.

back: Treat the URL as a serialized, public portion of navigation state: the path selects a resource or screen, the query selects a view, and the fragment identifies a position within the resulting document.
The browser owns session history even when a frontend router coordinates it.
examples: WHATWG, HTML Living Standard: Session history and navigation

back: Routers match paths, decode parameters, load data, enforce route-level policy, manage errors, and restore titles, focus, and scroll.
Authorization performed only in the router is bypassable, because the server remains the security authority.
Document navigation asks the server for a new top-level resource. Client navigation updates history and fetches or reveals the next screen without replacing the whole document.

prompt: A transfer form disables its submit control while the request is in flight. The network delivers that request twice anyway, and two transfers appear. What does that tell you about the two mechanisms involved?

options.text: Pending state prevents accidental repeated interaction; repeated network delivery is what an idempotency key handles
The pending state was implemented badly — a properly disabled control would have stopped the second delivery
options.feedback: A disabled control governs what the person can do. It sits on the wrong side of the wire to govern what happens to a request that has already left.

options.text: The server should have recognised the second request as a duplicate without being told
options.feedback: An idempotency key is how the second delivery is recognised as the same operation. Without one the two requests are indistinguishable.

options.text: They are two names for one guard, so one of them was redundant
options.feedback: They address different problems. Pending state prevents accidental repeated interaction, while an idempotency key handles repeated network delivery.

explanation: Pending state prevents accidental repeated interaction, while an idempotency key handles repeated network delivery — two mechanisms for two problems that look identical from outside. The transfer form in this lesson does both: it exposes pending status and submits a unique operation ID.

prompt: A submitted form comes back with every field empty, one field outlined in red and nothing else, and the words “invalid request” at the top. Which of the named form failures are on this screen?

options.text: A color-only error cue
A generic “invalid request” response, which prevents correction
Safe user input was not preserved after the rejected submission
Placeholder-only labels, which disappear
Client and server rules that have drifted apart

explanation: Three of the failures are visible here. Color-only error cues exclude users; generic “invalid request” responses prevent correction; and preserving safe user input after a rejected submission is exactly what emptying every field failed to do. The other two are real failures that nothing on this screen is evidence of — the fields may be labelled correctly, and one rejection is not a sign that the client and server rules disagree.

prompt: A transfer is submitted. Match each outcome to the response the form should give.

pairs.left: An amount in a format the form cannot parse
The destination account is not valid
pairs.right: an error mapped to that field

pairs.left: The request times out with an unknown outcome
pairs.right: an offer to look up the status

explanation: A transfer form parses an amount, announces inline format errors, and submits a unique operation ID. A declined transfer returns a form-level business message; an invalid destination maps to that field; an unknown timeout offers status lookup rather than a blind retry. The two distractors are the failures the design is avoiding — a blind retry on an outcome nobody knows, and a response the person cannot act on.

back: Client checks improve interaction; server checks protect authority; domain invariants preserve correctness. Each boundary validates for its own purpose.
Validation helps users correct input and protects application boundaries, but frontend validation never replaces backend validation or authorization.
Labels give controls names, input types and attributes express basic constraints, and submission serializes successful controls.
Optimistic completion feels fast but is unsuitable when the result is uncertain or costly to reverse.
Native HTML supplies submission and constraint-validation behavior that applications may progressively enhance; controlled component state offers coordination while native form state reduces code.

prompt: A settings screen writes a new display name into its own state the moment the reader clicks Save, before the server has answered. Which of these does that write still owe?

options.text: An idempotency key, so a repeated delivery is not a second effect
A rollback if the server rejects it
Invalidation of anything that summarised the old name
Deduplication against any other in-flight read of the same name
A cache key that leaves the account identity out, so every screen reads one entry

explanation: Mutations request effects and need explicit success semantics, idempotency, invalidation, and optimistic rollback. Optimistic updates improve responsiveness when rejection is rare and reversal is clear — the reversal is the rollback, and the invalidation is what stops a summary elsewhere from still showing the old name after confirmation. Deduplication is something queries can often have, because a read leaves nothing behind; and cache keys that omit identity or filters leak incorrect data.

prompt: A project page already holds the project's data in cache, marked stale, and a revalidation is under way. Two designs are proposed: cover the content with a loading overlay, or leave it visible under a small refresh indicator. What settles it?

options.text: Leave it visible — a loading overlay can erase usable stale content, and stale content is still content the reader can use
Cover it — showing data known to be stale is showing data known to be wrong
options.feedback: Stale is not wrong; it is aged. Remote state has two clocks, and the frontend's copy ageing is the normal condition rather than a fault.

options.text: Cover it — the overlay is how the reader learns a request is in flight
options.feedback: In-flight state does have to be visible, which is what an unobtrusive refresh indicator is for. It does not have to be made visible by hiding everything else.

options.text: Either — the choice is cosmetic, since the same data arrives at the same moment
options.feedback: The data does arrive at the same moment. What differs is how much of the wait the reader can do anything during, and a loading overlay can erase usable stale content for all of it.

explanation: A loading overlay can erase usable stale content. The project page here begins with cached project data marked stale, starts one revalidation, and renders an unobtrusive refresh indicator, which keeps both facts on the screen at once: this is what we have, and this is that it is being checked. A cache entry needs identity, value, freshness, and in-flight/error state, and freshness and in-flight state are the two the indicator is reporting.

prompt: A save times out with no answer. The client resends it automatically, three times, a second apart. What has that risked?

options.text: Duplicated mutations, and prolonging an overload that may have caused the timeout in the first place
Nothing, as long as the request carried an idempotency key
options.feedback: An idempotency key addresses the duplication. It does nothing about the second risk: automatic retries can prolong overload, and three more requests into a struggling server are three more requests.

options.text: Only the bandwidth of three extra requests
options.feedback: Automatic retries can duplicate mutations or prolong overload. Both of those are larger than the bandwidth.

options.text: An abort, since local interest in the first attempt has now lapsed
options.feedback: Abort signals end local interest, and nothing here aborted anything. The first attempt's outcome is still unknown, which is the whole difficulty.

explanation: Automatic retries can duplicate mutations or prolong overload. A timeout with no answer is not a failure but an unknown outcome, and resending is a decision to treat it as one — which is why mutations need explicit success semantics and idempotency before anything gets to retry them.

back: Remote state has two clocks: the server changes independently, and the frontend's copy ages. A cache entry therefore needs identity, value, freshness, and in-flight/error state.
Queries read representations and can often be deduplicated, cached, revalidated, or retried.

front: What a bad cache key costs
back: Cache keys that omit identity or filters leak incorrect data.
Fetch at route boundaries to avoid nested waterfalls, or near components to preserve ownership; many systems combine both with a shared query cache.
Polling is simple; server push is timely but operationally stateful.

prompt: A team ships a custom toggle: an element that is not a control, that responds to a click, and that turns green when it is on. Which of the four questions does it fail?

options.text: Can the user perceive the information? Its state is carried by color alone.
Can they operate it with available input? It is a clickable non-control.
Can assistive technologies determine names, roles, values, and updates? It has no control role for them to report.
Can they understand the state and consequences? The reader cannot tell what turning it on will do.

explanation: Ask four questions for every task: can the user perceive the information, can they operate it with available input, can they understand the state and consequences, and can assistive technologies determine names, roles, values, and updates. State conveyed only by color and clickable non-controls are both named failures, and semantic HTML is what communicates structure and control roles — so three of the four fail on one widget. Nothing in the description bears on the fourth, which is the point of asking four questions rather than reaching one verdict.

prompt: A long report finishes saving in the background while the reader is typing in a different field. How should the interface report it?

options.text: In a live region, which can announce asynchronous status without stealing focus
By moving focus to the confirmation message, so it is announced immediately
options.feedback: Focus identifies the active control, and the reader is using one. Moving focus mid-sentence takes the interface away from the task they are doing.

options.text: By turning the save indicator green
options.feedback: State conveyed only by color is a named failure, and it says nothing at all to a reader who is not looking at the indicator.

options.text: With a text alternative on the save icon
options.feedback: Text alternatives convey the purpose of non-text content — what the icon is for, not that something has just happened.

explanation: Live regions can announce asynchronous status without stealing focus, which is the property this situation needs: the status is asynchronous and the reader is in the middle of something. Focus does move elsewhere in the worked example, but only when the task itself moves — to an error summary after a failed submission, or to the new page heading after a successful one.

prompt: A redesign moves a summary panel to the top of the screen with CSS, leaving it last in the document. Readers who tab through the page still reach it last. Why?

options.text: Keyboard order follows DOM order unless it is deliberately managed
Because the panel is not a control, and only controls take keyboard order
options.feedback: The panel holds controls; the question is when they are reached, not whether. Keyboard order follows DOM order, and the CSS did not change the document.

options.text: Because focus indicators are hidden, so the panel is being reached earlier than it appears
options.feedback: Hidden focus indicators are a real failure, and they would make focus hard to see rather than change where it goes.

options.text: Because assistive technologies read visual position, and the panel has not been re-announced
options.feedback: The complaint is about tab order, which follows the document. Moving something visually does not move it in the DOM.

explanation: Keyboard order follows DOM order unless deliberately managed. A visual reordering done in CSS changes neither the document nor the order a keyboard traverses it in — one of the ways accessibility turns out to be a property of the complete interaction rather than a final audit step.

back: People with varied vision, hearing, mobility, cognition, devices, and input methods can perceive and operate the application. It is a property of the complete interaction, not a final audit step.
WCAG 2.2 organizes testable criteria under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust principles.
Visible labels or defined naming relationships.
Only a subset of the failures, which is why task-based manual testing remains necessary.
Native controls provide behavior and semantics at low cost; custom widgets may meet specialized needs but inherit keyboard, focus, state, and announcement obligations.

prompt: Complete the critical path this lesson uses.
explanation: The path is discover → connect → transfer → parse → execute → render → respond. Naming all seven keeps the word “performance” attached to a journey rather than to one stage: compression reduces transferred bytes, resource hints and document order affect discovery, code splitting defers code by route or capability, and long JavaScript tasks block input processing. Work not on the current critical path may still consume bandwidth, CPU, memory, and battery that delay important work.

prompt: A team halves the JavaScript an issue page ships. The measured time from navigation start to first responsive interaction does not move. What is the most likely reading?

options.text: The journey was not waiting on the stages a bundle governs — the critical path often crosses server, network, and browser boundaries
The measurement must be wrong, since shipping less JavaScript improves many devices
options.feedback: Shipping less JavaScript does improve many devices. That is a claim about a population of devices, not a promise about which stage this particular journey spends its time in.

options.text: The saving was cancelled out by the extra requests that splitting introduced
options.feedback: Excessive splitting does add requests and coordination, and it is worth checking. It is one specific hypothesis rather than the general reading, and it would tend to make the number worse rather than leave it unchanged.

options.text: Nothing can be concluded until the bundle is halved again
options.feedback: The point of measuring a user journey is that it answers questions, and this one answered: whatever the journey is waiting on, it is not the bytes that were removed.

explanation: Performance work should improve a measured user journey, not merely reduce a bundle or optimize an isolated function, and the critical path often crosses server, network, and browser boundaries. A bundle acts on transfer, parse and execute; if the journey is waiting on discovery, connection, or the server behind them, removing half of it changes nothing the reader experiences.

prompt: A dashboard reports that the average load time for the issue page improved again this quarter. The complaints did not. What is the average hiding?

options.text: Slow cohorts and the long tail — the average moved without them moving
Nothing — an average over enough journeys is the journey
options.feedback: Averages hide slow cohorts and long tails. More journeys make the average steadier, not more representative of the slowest ones.

options.text: The lab measurements, which were taken on fast machines
options.feedback: Lab tests on fast machines do hide real-device problems, and that is a separate failure. This number came from real journeys; what went wrong is how they were summarised.

options.text: Third-party scripts, whose time is not attributed to the page
options.feedback: Third-party scripts block critical work, so their cost is inside these journeys rather than outside them. The summarising is what lost the slow readers.

explanation: Averages hide slow cohorts and long tails. That is one half of the puzzle this lesson opened with, and it has a companion in the other: lab tests on fast machines hide real-device problems. Both produce a number that is true and unrepresentative, which is why performance work should improve a measured user journey rather than a summary that has already averaged the journey away.

back: The user's experience of loading, seeing, and operating an interface: network latency, resource priority, parsing, JavaScript execution, rendering stability, and interaction responsiveness.

front: Off the critical path is not free
back: Work not on the current critical path may still consume bandwidth, CPU, memory, and battery that delay important work.
Hydration can duplicate server work or make controls appear before they function.
Long JavaScript tasks block input processing. Browser rendering and scheduling determine when content is usable, which is a different question from when it arrived.
Shipping less JavaScript improves many devices, but excessive splitting adds requests and coordination.

prompt: An endpoint that resizes images is added to an event-driven service. It works. But three unrelated endpoints on the same service — none of them touching images — get much slower at the same time. What accounts for that?

options.text: CPU work can stall all requests on that loop, and blocking an event loop inflates unrelated latency
The resizing is holding a thread from the pool, so fewer threads are left for the rest
options.feedback: That is how a thread-per-request runtime would fail: thread pools isolate blocking work until the pool is exhausted. This runtime multiplexes many I/O operations through loops and callbacks, so there is no per-request thread to hold.

options.text: Leaked thread-local or global state is crossing requests
options.feedback: That failure shows up as one request seeing another's data. It does not make endpoints that share nothing get slower together.

options.text: Unbounded concurrency has exhausted memory or downstream connections
options.feedback: Unbounded concurrency exhausts memory or downstream connections, and that is a failure of admission. Nothing here says either ran out; what changed is that CPU work joined the loop.

explanation: Event loops efficiently wait on I/O but CPU work can stall all requests on a loop, and blocking an event loop inflates unrelated latency. The unrelated endpoints are the evidence: they did nothing different, they share the loop, and the loop is where the resizing went. Concurrency should match workload — which is why the image endpoint in this lesson delegates resizing to a bounded CPU worker pool instead.

prompt: A deploy replaces the image service. The old process stops admission, waits within a deadline, then exits. Which of these does that sequence achieve?

options.text: New work stops entering before the waiting begins
The wait has an upper bound, so the exit is certain
It avoids the dropped in-flight work that an abrupt shutdown causes
Every request already admitted is guaranteed to finish
The CPU worker pool is freed immediately, so the replacement can start resizing

explanation: Shutdown stops admission, waits within a deadline, then exits — which is this runtime's answer to “how is a process stopped without abandoning work?” Stopping admission first is what makes the wait finite; the deadline is what makes the exit certain; and the point of both is that abrupt shutdown drops in-flight work. The deadline is also why nothing is guaranteed to finish: it bounds the wait rather than the work. And nothing here frees the pool early — the wait exists precisely so the pool can drain.

prompt: A team is deciding how the image service should run. Match each choice to what it trades.

pairs.left: Send blocking work to a thread pool
pairs.right: blocking work isolated, until the pool is exhausted
better isolation and CPU use, at more memory and coordination
automatic reclamation, traded for pause and memory behavior

distractors: many I/O operations multiplexed through loops and callbacks
explanation: Thread pools isolate blocking work until the pool is exhausted. More processes improve isolation and CPU use while increasing memory and coordination. Garbage-collected runtimes trade automatic reclamation for pause and memory behavior; manual-memory runtimes trade control for safety obligations. The two distractors are not trades at all — they describe how event-driven runtimes and actor or lightweight-task models schedule work, which is a different question from what a choice costs.

back: It loads application code, accepts work, schedules execution, manages memory and I/O, and integrates with the operating system. Language syntax is only one part of its operational behavior.

front: The five questions every runtime answers
back: How does work enter? How many requests run concurrently? What blocks progress? Where is mutable state? How is a process stopped without abandoning work?
Between network-facing server software and application code. It may directly accept HTTP, run behind a dedicated proxy, or execute functions in a managed platform.
They restart failed instances and coordinate signals.
Long-lived processes reuse pools and caches; function platforms simplify lifecycle but can add startup and connection churn.

prompt: Put the first six steps of the backend request lifecycle in order.

steps.text: Parse, applying size and syntax limits

explanation: The pipeline runs parse → establish deadline/trace → authenticate → route → authorize → validate → execute use case → serialize → observe. Some steps overlap, but their responsibilities remain distinct, and two adjacencies carry most of the argument. Routing sits between authentication and authorization because authentication establishes identity while authorization checks the requested effect, and the effect being checked is the one the selected handler names. Validation comes after both because it converts transport data to typed input — meaning rather than shape.

prompt: `PATCH /profiles/42` is reachable only by an authenticated caller, and the router enforces that. A caller with a valid session updates profile `42`, which is not theirs. Which step was skipped?

options.text: Authorization — the check on the requested effect, as opposed to on the route
Authentication — the session was never really established
options.feedback: Authentication establishes identity, and it worked: the caller had a valid session. Knowing who someone is has never been the same as knowing what they may do.

options.text: Validation — the profile id was never converted to typed input
options.feedback: Validation converts transport data to typed input. A well-typed `42` is still `42`; the problem is not the shape of the id but whose profile it names.

options.text: Parsing — size and syntax limits would have caught it
options.feedback: Parsing applies size and syntax limits, and a small, well-formed request passes both. Those limits bound the message, not the effect.

explanation: Authentication establishes identity; authorization checks the requested effect — and authorizing only at route level is one of the recurring errors of this pipeline. The worked example is explicit about the difference: `PATCH /profiles/42` authenticates the session and then checks permission for profile `42`, not permission for the route.

prompt: In the `PATCH /profiles/42` example, a uniqueness conflict becomes a stable `409` and an unexpected database error becomes an opaque `500` tied to a trace ID. Which of these does that mapping get right?

options.text: The conflict gets a stable status, so the caller can act on it
The unexpected error is opaque, so internals do not leak
The opaque response carries a trace ID, so it stays diagnosable
Both become the same status, so callers have only one case to handle
The database error message is passed through, so the caller can see what failed

explanation: Error mapping produces stable HTTP status semantics without leaking internals. The two halves are not in tension: a uniqueness conflict is something the application understands and refuses, so it gets a stable `409`; an unexpected database error is not, so it becomes an opaque `500` tied to a trace ID. Collapsing both into one status throws away the first half, and passing the database message through throws away the second. Request context carries correlation, which is what keeps an opaque response findable.

back: An untrusted protocol message into an authorized application operation, and then into a bounded response.
It can convert programming defects into misleading business responses.
It simplifies atomicity but holds locks during remote calls.
It centralizes repeated policy, but order becomes significant.
Streaming reduces buffering but prevents changing the status after headers are sent.

prompt: `approveExpense` is changed to read the current time and the current user from globals rather than receiving them. The rules it enforces are otherwise unchanged. What has that cost?

options.text: The logic becomes hard to test, because time and current user are now read globally rather than supplied
Nothing — the rule is still enforced in one place, which was the point
options.feedback: It is still in one place. But this layer keeps dependencies directed toward application policy, with ports for data, time, messages, and external services; a global read is a dependency pointing the other way, and time, randomness, and current user read globally make logic hard to test.

options.text: The use case now owns rules that belong to domain objects
options.feedback: A use case owns the workflow; domain objects or functions own rules that remain true regardless of interface. Reading a clock changes neither ownership.

options.text: The database schema will start leaking into the public API
options.feedback: Database schemas leaking into public APIs is a separate named failure, and it is about what the API exposes. Nothing here changed what the API returns.

explanation: Time, randomness, and current user are read globally, making logic hard to test — one of the named failure modes of this layer. The repair is in the mental model: ports for data, time, messages, and external services, so the use case is handed what it depends on instead of reaching for it. That is what keeping dependencies directed toward application policy means in practice.

prompt: `approveExpense` must now also register the approval in an external system that commits separately. Which of these follow?

options.text: The approver-and-limit invariant still belongs inside one transaction
The part that crosses systems needs explicit intermediate states
The part that crosses systems needs compensation
The external registration should happen before commit, so it is never missed
The invariant should move into the HTTP handler, so every caller enforces it

explanation: Strong invariants often belong inside one transaction; cross-system processes require explicit intermediate states and compensation, because the crossing part has no single commit to hide inside. The example already shows the shape: `approveExpense` records approval and schedules notification after commit rather than before it. Moving the invariant into the handler is the opposite move — anemic models scatter rules through controllers, and HTTP maps input to the command precisely so a worker can invoke the same use case without duplicating rules.

prompt: A repository interface has one implementation, and each of its methods corresponds one-to-one with a database call. A reviewer proposes deleting it and calling the database from the use case. What settles it?

options.text: Whether the separation adds value — abstractions protect stable business language, but are wasteful when they merely rename a database call
Keep it — repositories or ports always belong between a use case and storage
options.feedback: The guidance is conditional: repositories or ports hide storage operations when that separation adds value. “Always” is not the claim.

options.text: Delete it — an abstraction between application policy and storage inverts the dependency direction
options.feedback: Ports are how dependencies stay directed toward application policy. They are the mechanism, not a violation of it; what is in question is whether this particular one is doing anything.

options.text: Keep it — deleting it would make the model anemic
options.feedback: Anemic models scatter rules through controllers. Where a storage call is made is a different question from where the rules live.

explanation: Abstractions protect stable business language but are wasteful when they merely rename a database call, and repositories or ports hide storage operations when that separation adds value. Both sentences are conditional, and the condition is the answer: the test is not whether an abstraction exists but whether it is protecting the vocabulary of the problem from the vocabulary of the storage.

back: Domain logic expresses rules that make the application meaningful; application logic coordinates those rules with persistence, identity, time, and external systems.
Commands express requested effects; queries retrieve views.
Value objects represent validated concepts such as money or email addresses; entities carry identity across change.
Rich models colocate state and rules; procedural services can be clearer for workflows spanning many entities.

front: A rule enforced only in the UI
back: It is bypassed by another client.

prompt: A request starts work that will outlive it. Put the four steps in order.

steps.text: A durable intent or record is written
A reference to it is enqueued

explanation: The flow is request → durable intent/record → enqueue reference → worker effect, with an immediate status response going back to the caller and progress or a result available afterwards. The order carries the central claim: the database record is often the authority and the queue is a delivery mechanism, so the record exists before anything is enqueued, and what gets enqueued is a reference rather than the data itself.

prompt: A handler writes a record and enqueues a job for it. A worker occasionally starts and finds no record. A developer proposes moving the enqueue after the commit. What does that buy, and what does it cost?

options.text: It closes the window where a worker observes missing data, and opens one where the notification is lost — unless an outbox or repair process covers it
It closes the window entirely, since after a commit the record is durable
options.feedback: Half right. The record is durable, so no worker can miss it. What is now unprotected is the enqueue itself: committing before enqueue can lose the notification without an outbox or repair process.

options.text: It costs nothing, because at-least-once delivery will redeliver the job
options.feedback: At-least-once delivery is a property of messages the queue has accepted. A message that was never enqueued is not one the queue can repeat.

options.text: It buys nothing, because the queue is the authority for whether the work happened
options.feedback: The database record is often the authority; the queue is a delivery mechanism. Keeping the authority ahead of the delivery is exactly what the proposal is trying to do.

explanation: Enqueuing before a transaction commits can let a worker observe missing data; committing before enqueue can lose the notification without an outbox or repair process. Neither ordering is free, which is why the worked example refuses to choose between them: completion records the object and an outbox event in one transaction, so the fact and its delivery become durable together.

prompt: A requirement says that signing a user out must take effect immediately, everywhere. Which of these follow for the session design?

options.text: Server-side sessions suit the requirement, because they are revocable
Server-side sessions require shared storage
Self-contained tokens complicate revocation
Self-contained tokens suit it better, because they reduce lookups
Either design meets it, since both carry identity across stateless requests

explanation: Server-side sessions are revocable and small on the client but require shared storage; self-contained tokens reduce lookups but complicate revocation and claim freshness. The requirement picks a side of that trade rather than dissolving it, and shared storage is the price. Reducing lookups is the same property as complicating revocation, seen from the other end: a session identifier maps a browser credential to server-side state, or a signed token carries selected claims — both carry identity, and only one of them can be told that the identity's access has ended.

back: They preserve user-associated state across stateless HTTP requests. A session identifier maps a browser credential to server-side state, or a signed token carries selected claims.

front: How an upload should be handled
back: Streamed, type-checked by content and policy, scanned where appropriate, and stored under a generated name.
Leasing or acknowledgement, retries, delay, and dead-letter handling.
Because at-least-once delivery can repeat work.
They save backend bandwidth but need scoped authorization.

prompt: Through an afternoon, requests take steadily longer while the number completing per second barely moves and no error rate has changed. What is the best reading of that?

options.text: Utilization is approaching a limit: queueing grows as it does, so latency often fails before throughput stops
Nothing is wrong yet — throughput measures capacity, and it has not moved
options.feedback: Throughput moving last is the problem rather than the reassurance. Queueing grows as utilization approaches a limit, so latency often fails before throughput stops; a flat throughput graph is compatible with a service already in trouble.

options.text: A dependency has failed, and circuit breaking has not engaged
options.feedback: Circuit breaking stops repeatedly calling a failing dependency, and a failing dependency would show up somewhere in the error rate. Nothing here has failed; everything is merely slower.

options.text: State is stored on one instance, so load balancing has become inconsistent
options.feedback: State stored on one instance makes load balancing and failover inconsistent, which shows as requests behaving differently depending on where they land — not as everything slowing together.

explanation: Capacity is bounded at every resource — CPU, memory, worker slots, connections, storage I/O, and dependency quotas — and queueing grows as utilization approaches a limit, so latency often fails before throughput stops. Steady throughput with rising latency is that claim seen from the outside, which is why both scaling and resilience begin with measured constraints rather than with multiplying services.

prompt: A shop page is being hardened against a failing recommendation service. Match each measure to what it does.

pairs.right: rejects excess work before all requests time out
stops repeatedly calling a failing dependency
preserves core tasks by omitting optional dependencies

distractors: adds instances when work can be distributed
lets any healthy instance serve a request
explanation: Load shedding rejects excess work before all requests time out. Deadlines bound resource use. Circuit breaking stops repeatedly calling a failing dependency. Bulkheads reserve capacity between workloads. Graceful degradation preserves core tasks by omitting optional dependencies. The two distractors describe horizontal scaling and stateless request handling — both about serving more work, neither about behaving well when there is less. The shop page uses three of the five: a short deadline, degradation to products without recommendations, and core inventory and checkout capacity kept isolated from optional personalization traffic.

prompt: A dependency starts failing with intermittent resets. A team adds an immediate retry on every failed call, with no limit. Load rises. What is the likely result?

options.text: A retry storm — one of the mechanisms by which a local problem becomes a cascading failure
Improved transient success, since resets are exactly what retries are for
options.feedback: Retries improve transient success only with backoff, jitter, budgets, and idempotency. An immediate, unlimited retry has none of the four.
